newsitem.title: TURKEY: FUTURES--Turkey says market will open despite row.
newsitem.headline: FUTURES--Turkey says market will open despite row.

text.p: Turkey's first futures market, which will initially trade cotton contracts, will be opened soon despite a lingering dispute between government bodies over its control and regulation, senior officials said.
"Work to launch a futures market under the umbrella of Izmir Trade Bourse is at its final stage," Industry Minister Yalim Erez told parliament.
"The legislation of the market is ready," he said of the Izmir Futures Mercantile Exchange (IFME), the first futures market to be set up in Turkey.
The establishment of the exchange was disputed earlier this year by the government's securities watchdog, the Capital Markets Board (SPK).
The SPK recently filed a suit in the Council of State, the highest arbitrator in Turkey, to end the dispute.
The disagreement between the SPK and the Izmir Trade Bourse (ITB) stemmed from control over futures transactions, which the SPK says are a securities tool and therefore must be controlled by itself.
The SPK also says it is the sole authority to set up any commodity futures exchanges in Turkey.

But the ITB and the industry ministry -- which sides with the ITB in the issue and prepared the legislation published in the Official Gazette which took effect in August -- say the SPK should only audit and inspect trading procedures, but should not meddle with the establishment of the market.
Hasan Ozmen, head of the ITB, said on Thursday he believed the dispute would be resolved soon and the market would be opened in 1997.

"I think the dispute will be over very soon. If not, we will go ahead with our plans and begin operating the market. We have the backing from the government," he told Reuters on the sidelines of a futures markets seminar in Ankara.

"We are now at the stage of installing the computer system and software from an international company. Everything else is almost ready and the next step is to choose the brokerage houses and train them on computer simulations," he said.
The ITB, which already runs the oldest cash market in Turkey for cotton, raisins, dry figs and other crops, masterminded the futures market plan as early as 1991 after approval from the World Bank.

It aims at attracting standard cotton from all over Turkey, some neighbouring countries and later Central Asian republics, and also making good-quality cotton at international prices available to the local textile sector.
Turkey is the sixth largest cotton producer in the world with annual production of 837,000 tonnes in 1995/96.
Ozmen said the local textile sector would boom if the market began operating because it would allow producers and industrial buyers to see future prices clearly.
"There is not any reason why textile exports should not double if the futures markets is opened," he said.
Ozmen said the next contract to be traded on the exchange would be olive oil or raisins.
